A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Picard Iteration research. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support comparison despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original fulfillment simulations, end-to-end policy optimization experiments, MuJoCo convergence results, and a capacity-dependence ablation.

after.justification: v2 retains original fulfillment and MuJoCo experiments and adds inventory-replenishment simulations and sensitivity analyses in Appendix B.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same parallel simulation, cached-action updates, feasibility fallback, and convergence rule. Restart and chunking optimizations are relocated. The replenishment application selects retailer-based partitions within the existing general algorithm.

E1.justification: Appendix B adds an evaluated One Warehouse Multi-Retailer inventory-control task with warehouse and retailer replenishment, extending beyond allocation of existing inventory in fulfillment optimization. The fulfillment and eight MuJoCo environments remain; Appendix C's capacity-refresh extension is theoretical.

E2.justification: The end-to-end experiment no longer reports comparisons against the greedy starting policy: Table 2 removes its improvement-over-greedy column. Sequential simulation and the tailored GPU Time Warp comparator remain. The new replenishment benchmark also uses sequential simulation.

E3.justification: Appendix B.3 introduces a year-long replenishment protocol with 3.65M events, 4,000 workers, a width-512 MLP, max_steps=130, and parameter sweeps. Table 2 drops the policy-improvement metric and two problem scales. The fulfillment demand formula changes from i^{-beta} to i^{beta}; this corrects the reported specification without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix B.3 adds sensitivity analyses testing demand skew, retailer count, batch size, and neural-network width through Table 4 and Figures 4–5. These examine load imbalance and scaling limitations in replenishment. The existing capacity-dependent-policy ablation in Appendix A.4 is unchanged.

E5.justification: The MuJoCo analysis retains medians over 30 seeds and 20th–80th percentile bands in v1 Figure 2 and v2 Figure 3. The new replenishment results introduce no reported repeated-run counts, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests.

E6.justification: New replenishment results include a 230x base-case speedup, 33x at alpha=0.011, and a 383x peak at 1,000 workers. Table 2 removes greedy-policy gains and the 3k/1k and 30M/10M rows, while adding runtime ratios. Retained fulfillment and MuJoCo findings are unchanged; rounded sequential runtimes do not establish performance changes.

T1.justification: Appendix B introduces replenishment dynamics, restricted policy assumptions, and Theorem B.1's 2R iteration bound, where R counts warehouse replenishments, supported by Lemma B.2 and a proof sketch. Appendix C adds a capacity-refresh complexity bound O(T(K+J)M/P) and a reduction argument. The original fulfillment guarantees and proofs are retained.

C1.justification: Replenishment changes from proposed future work in v1 Section 6 to a claimed demonstrated application with empirical and theoretical speedups in v2 Sections 3 and 6. The central Picard contribution, approximately 400x fulfillment speedup, and potential MuJoCo acceleration remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Section 1.1 adds a substantive explanation of Time Warp's difficulties through dense communication, cascading rollbacks, and GPU overhead. Appendix B explains replenishment-specific applicability restrictions and attributes declining speedups to demand imbalance and possibly GPU memory. The existing cheap-dynamics requirement and MuJoCo caveats remain.

D1.justification: v2 documents replenishment configurations, including worker count, network width, and chunk size. Existing JAX, A100, precision, and optimization details largely move to Appendix A.3. However, the fulfillment setting max_steps=300M disappears, and the direct code-repository link becomes a nonspecific supplementary-material reference.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting its expanded Time Warp discussion, including Jefferson (1985), Fujimoto (1990, 2024), and Radhakrishnan et al. (1996), plus replenishment references such as Dehaybe et al. (2024) and Scarf et al. (1960). Its principal positioning relative to parallel RL and discrete-event simulation remains.

P1.justification: The introduction is reorganized around a new 'Time Warp Falls Short' subsection, related work gains thematic subdivisions, and implementation material moves from the main experiments section to Appendix A.3. The experimental narrative is condensed and rewritten, alongside revised headings and author information.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. v2 adds the explanatory Figure 1, replenishment Figures 4–5 and Table 4, separates the formerly adjacent fulfillment plot and table, and restructures Table 2. Existing fulfillment and MuJoCo plots are resized and relocated.

improvement.justification: The replenishment experiments and sensitivity analyses support an application that v1 left as future work, while Figure 1 and the revised introduction clarify the comparison with Time Warp. These provide a limited net gain: the core method and results remain stable, the new OWMR proof is only sketched, and v2 loses greedy-policy comparisons, the partly estimated largest-scale timing row, and a direct code link.
